# Systemic sclerosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Restrictive lung diseases > Systemic sclerosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/eT0xp2)

---

## Summary

Systemic <u>sclerosis</u> (SSc) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy and <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>skin</u> and other organs. Based on the extent of cutaneous involvement, SSc is categorized as limited or diffuse. <u>Limited SSc</u>, which is more common, begins with cutaneous <u>sclerosis</u> of the fingers, hands, and face, which then progresses proximally toward the center of the body. Cutaneous involvement may be followed by internal organ involvement 10–20 years after disease onset. <u>Diffuse SSc</u>, which is less common, may be life-threatening in individuals with early involvement of the <u>heart</u>, <u>lungs</u>, or <u>kidneys</u>. The term <u>CREST syndrome</u> (<u>calcinosis cutis</u>, <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>, <u>esophageal dysmotility</u>, <u>sclerodactyly</u>, and <u>telangiectasia</u>) has historically been used to describe a group of symptoms that are typically present in patients with <u>limited SSc</u>; however, these symptoms may also be seen in patients with <u>diffuse SSc</u>. Treatment is symptomatic and based on the extent of <u>skin</u> and internal organ involvement. A multidisciplinary approach is recommended to address the complex and heterogeneous manifestations of SSc. <u>Scleroderma renal crisis</u> (<u>SRC</u>) is a life-threatening complication of SSc characterized by the abrupt onset of <u>hypertension</u> and <u>oliguric</u> <u>AKI</u>. <u>Management of SRC</u> includes initiation or uptitration of <u>ACE inhibitors</u> and nephrology consultation. Cardiopulmonary complications of SSc are common and require management of the specific condition as well as possible additional <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>. The prognosis varies depending on organ involvement; <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u> (<u>PAH</u>), <u>interstitial lung disease</u> (<u>ILD</u>), and cardiac disease significantly increase the <u>mortality rate</u>.

## Epidemiology

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 5:1)  [[1]](/library/gQXFvB)[[2]](/library/NQX-wB)

* Higher <u>incidence</u> in African Americans [[1]](/library/gQXFvB)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–50 years [[3]](/library/4QX3wB)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

The pathophysiology of SSc is not completely understood, but several factors play a role in the development of the disease.




* Autoimmunologic component (see “Diagnostics”)

* Inflammatory synthesis of <u>extracellular matrix</u>: <u>fibroblast</u> <u>proliferation</u> and increased synthesis of normal <u>collagen</u> leading to <u>fibrosis</u>

* Noninflammatory vasculopathy: underlying mechanism of many of the more severe disease features, e.g., <u>CAD</u>, <u>pulmonary artery hypertension</u>, and renal crisis





References:[[4]](/library/GeYBZo)

## Clinical features

### Overview [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)[[6]](/library/wxchAe0)




SSc is most commonly described as limited or diffuse based on the cutaneous manifestations and symptom progression. [[7]](/library/zR1rpg0)




| <br>Common SSc subtypes<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Limited SSc | Diffuse SSc |
| Cutaneous distribution | <br><br>* Neck, face, and <u>distal</u> limbs<br><br>* Sparing of the trunk<br><br><br> | <br>* Trunk, face, and extremities<br><br> |
| <br>Extracutaneous manifestations [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)<br> | <br>* May occur<br><br>* <u>PAH</u><br><br>* Severe gastrointestinal involvement (e.g., <u>bloating</u>, <u>constipation</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Commonly occur<br><br>* <u>Scleroderma renal crisis</u><br><br>* Cardiac involvement<br><br>* <u>ILD</u><br><br> |
| <br>Onset of systemic symptoms [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)<br> | <br>* Slow: years after <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u><br><br> | <br>* Rapid: simultaneously with <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u> or within weeks to months<br><br> |





### CREST syndrome




<u>CREST syndrome</u> refers to a constellation of symptoms traditionally associated with <u>limited SSc</u> (can also be seen in <u>diffuse SSc</u>).




* C: Calcinosis cutis: small white <u>calcium</u> deposits on the pressure points of the extremities (e.g., <u>elbows</u>, knees, fingertips)

* R: <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* E: Esophageal hypomotility (systemic sclerosis): <u>smooth muscle</u> <u>atrophy</u> and <u>fibrosis</u> → <u>esophageal dysmotility</u> and decreased <u>lower esophageal sphincter</u> pressure → <u>dysphagia</u>, <u>gastroesophageal reflux</u>, <u>heartburn</u> → <u>aspiration</u>, <u>Barrett esophagus</u>, stricture

* S: <u>Sclerodactyly</u>

* T: <u>Telangiectasia</u>

### Cutaneous [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Thickening and hardening of the <u>skin</u>, which appears smooth, shiny, and puffy

* Sclerodactyly: <u>fibrotic</u> thickening and tightening of the <u>skin</u> on the fingers and hands 

* <u>Edema</u> followed by <u>fibrosis</u> that results in a waxy appearance of the <u>skin</u>

* Limited <u>range of motion</u> and possibly flexure <u>contractures</u> and clawing of the digits

* Red-blue discoloration of the fingers

* Multiple, painful <u>ischemic</u> digital <u>ulcers</u> with <u>atrophy</u> and <u>necrotic</u> spots

* Digital pitting: <u>hyperkeratotic</u> scarring that most commonly affects the fingertips

* Lesions on the <u>proximal</u> <u>nail fold</u>

* Depigmentation with sparing of perifollicular pigmentation (salt-and-pepper appearance)

* Face changes

* Loss of expression (mask-like facies)

* Smoothing of deep <u>wrinkles</u>

* Microstomia (a disproportionately small mouth) accompanied by characteristic perioral <u>wrinkles</u>

* Shortened frenulum

### Renal




* <u>Scleroderma renal crisis</u> (<u>SRC</u>): <u>medical emergency</u>, see “<u>Management of SRC</u>.”

* Presents in 10–15% of individuals with <u>diffuse SSc</u> and 1–2% of individuals with <u>limited SSc</u>

* Clinical features of SRC

* <u>Oliguric</u> <u>acute kidney injury</u>, <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>hematuria</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u> with or without <u>symptoms of hypertensive emergency</u>

* <u>Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia</u> (<u>MAHA</u>) and <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* Treatment: <u>ACE inhibitors</u>

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>: reduced <u>kidney function</u> due to abnormal <u>collagen</u> deposition → thickening of renal arteriolar walls → decreased <u>renal blood flow</u>





### Cardiopulmonary [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[9]](/library/_uY5FI)[[10]](/library/Ky1UTj0)[[11]](/library/6y1jTj0)




The <u>heart</u> and <u>lungs</u> are commonly affected by SSc, but usually remain asymptomatic in the early stages of the disease. Overt cardiopulmonary symptoms are associated with poor outcomes. [[12]](/library/qC1CGQ0)[[13]](/library/IC1YtQ0)




* Cardiovascular [[10]](/library/Ky1UTj0)[[11]](/library/6y1jTj0)

* Primary cardiac involvement

* <u>Endomyocardial fibrosis</u>

* <u>Myocarditis</u>

* <u>Pericarditis</u>

* Conduction disease and <u>arrhythmias</u>, e.g., <u>Afib</u>

* <u>HFpEF</u>

* <u>Pericardial effusion</u>

* Secondary involvement: due to <u>PAH</u>, <u>renal failure</u>, <u>amyloidosis</u>

* Pulmonary [[9]](/library/_uY5FI)

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u>

* <u>Pulmonary artery hypertension</u>

* Other: <u>ARDS</u>, <u>diffuse alveolar hemorrhage</u>, <u>aspiration pneumonitis</u>





### Other extracutaneous [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)




* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u>

* Esophageal dysmotility → <u>dysphagia</u> and reflux

* <u>Small bowel</u> dysmotility → <u>bloating</u>, gas, <u>constipation</u>, and cramping

* Vascular disease

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Thromboembolism</u>

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>

* <u>Arthralgia</u> and <u>myalgia</u>: may develop into <u>contractures</u>

* Other

* Fatigue, <u>weakness</u>, <u>pain</u>

* Weight loss  [[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)

* <u>Sicca syndrome</u>, <u>hypothyroidism</u>

* Increased risk of cancer and adverse fetal outcomes

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)




Consult rheumatology for all patients.




* SSc is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* <u>Skin</u> thickening on both hands that extends <u>proximal</u> to the <u>MCP joints</u> is diagnostic.

* Multiple organ system involvement is a hallmark.

* Perform a comprehensive evaluation to determine disease severity.

* Obtain routine <u>laboratory studies</u> and SSc-specific evaluations.

* Assess for cardiopulmonary complications (even if asymptomatic).

* Consider additional studies to monitor for organ involvement.

* Classification criteria for SSc can help identify SSc  . [[15]](/library/-R1Dpg0)





> [!TIP]
> Organ involvement typically occurs early in the course of SSc. [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Scleroderma renal crisis</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u> with a high <u>mortality rate</u>. Promptly evaluate serum <u>creatinine</u> and urine protein in individuals with SSc who present with an acute rise in blood pressure and start <u>management of SRC</u>. [[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)




![Scleroderma/Systemic Sclerosis (2013 EULAR/ACR Criteria)](media/qw0ewfqnvrtyi6v5r6rlguiz.jpg)

Scleroderma/Systemic Sclerosis (2013 EULAR/ACR Criteria)




### Routine evaluations [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)




Obtain the following studies in all patients with suspected SSc.




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>Renal function testing</u>

* ↑ Serum <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> disturbances

* ↑ Spot <u>urine protein/creatinine ratio</u> in <u>SRC</u>

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: ↑ <u>CRP</u>, ↑ <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Antinuclear antibodies</u> (<u>ANA</u>): present in ∼ 90% of patients [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)

* SSc-specific <u>autoantibodies</u>  [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)

* Anticentromere antibodies: associated with <u>limited SSc</u>, increased risk for vascular complications (e.g., <u>PAH</u>)

* Anti-Scl-70 (<u>anti-topoisomerase I antibody</u>): associated with severe and rapidly progressive <u>diffuse SSc</u>, <u>limited SSc</u>, <u>ILD</u>, digital <u>ulcers</u>

* Anti-RNA polymerase III: associated with <u>diffuse SSc</u>, <u>scleroderma renal crisis</u>

* <u>BNP</u>: to detect cardiopulmonary disease

* <u>Nailfold capillaroscopy</u>: <u>Microvascular</u> abnormalities are observed in ∼ 97% of individuals with SSc.  [[16]](/library/6V1jvf0)

* Cardiopulmonary assessment: Obtain baseline testing and refer to a specialist for further testing. [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)

* <u>ECG</u> or <u>Holter monitor</u>: <u>arrhythmia</u> due to <u>fibrosis</u>

* <u>Echocardiogram</u> (<u>TTE</u>): <u>diastolic</u> and/or <u>systolic heart failure</u>, <u>pericardial effusion</u>, <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>

* <u>High-resolution CT</u> (<u>HRCT</u>) chest: findings suggestive of <u>ILD</u> (e.g., reticular opacities, <u>fibrosis</u>)

* <u>Pulmonary function testing</u>: typically ↓ <u>FVC</u> and ↓ <u>DLCO</u>





> [!TIP]
> Consider early diagnostic testing to uncover silent disease.




![Nailfold capillaroscopy](media/mm7gv62hae316lghbh26vuwo.jpg)

Nailfold capillaroscopy

![Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)](media/xqwnb99jgxwaffnu0ndqidno.jpg)

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)




### Additional studies [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)




Depending on the patient's clinical features and <u>risk factors</u>, consider the following studies:




* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u> studies (e.g., <u>EGD</u>, <u>gastric emptying study</u>): e.g., to rule out <u>GERD</u> or dysmotility

* <u>Right heart catheterization</u>: when clinical <u>features of PH</u> or <u>anticentromere antibody</u> positive <u>serology</u> (associated with <u>PAH</u>) are present

* <u>Cardiac MRI</u>: for patients with <u>diffuse SSc</u> (associated with cardiac involvement)





> [!TIP]
> Upper <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> involvement is observed in almost all patients who have had SSc for > 10 years.

## Treatment

### General principles [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)[[17]](/library/eycxVU0)




* Refer to a specialist early.

* Treatment focuses on organ-specific, symptomatic therapy.

* In diffuse cutaneous disease or severe organ involvement, <u>systemic immunomodulatory medication</u> is indicated.

* Monitor for organ involvement and complications frequently to reduce mortality. [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)





### Cutaneous disease [[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[17]](/library/eycxVU0)




* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u> (RP)

* First line: <u>calcium channel blockers</u>, e.g., <u>nifedipine</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* Severe or refractory RP: add oral <u>PDE</u>–5 inhibitors (e.g., <u>sildenafil</u>) or IV <u>iloprost</u>

* Digital <u>ulceration</u> (DU)

* First line: <u>PDE-5 inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>tadalafil</u>) or IV <u>iloprost</u>

* Severe or refractory DU: Consider <u>bosentan</u>.

* Cutaneous <u>fibrosis</u>

* Early <u>diffuse SSc</u>; : <u>phototherapy</u>, and/or pharmacotherapy (e.g., <u>methotrexate</u>, or <u>mycophenolate mofetil</u>)

* Severe or refractory <u>fibrosis</u>: <u>cyclophosphamide</u> or <u>autologous HSCT</u>

* <u>Calcinosis cutis</u>: carbon dioxide laser, or surgical removal of symptomatic lesions





#### <u>Supportive care</u> [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[18]](/library/1yc2VU0)




* Avoid hand trauma and exposure to cold (e.g., by using gloves).

* Prevent dry <u>skin</u> (e.g., with warm oil, paraffin baths, <u>emollients</u>).

* Encourage <u>smoking cessation</u>.  [[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)

* Consider <u>vasodilatory</u> <u>physical therapy</u> and <u>lymph</u> drainage.

* Offer <u>antihistamines</u> for treatment of <u>pruritus</u>.

* Avoid <u>beta blockers</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>beta blockers</u>, which can cause vasospasm and may worsen <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u> and digital <u>ischemia</u> in patients with SSc. [[14]](/library/yxcd_e0)




### Renal disease




* <u>Scleroderma renal crisis</u>

* <u>ACE inhibitors</u> (<u>ACEIs</u>) are the mainstay of therapy

* <u>Captopril</u> is most commonly used

* See “<u>Management of SRC</u>.”

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>: See “<u>Management of CKD</u>.”





### Cardiopulmonary disease




Manage specific cardiac and/or pulmonary conditions depending on manifestations (see “Clinical features”).




* <u>Heart</u> disease: depending on specific manifestation

* See “<u>Treatment of heart failure</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade</u>.”

* See “<u>Management of acute heart failure</u>.”

* See “Treatment of <u>atrial fibrillation</u>.”

* See “<u>Restrictive cardiomyopathy</u>.”

* Pulmonary disease

* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u>

* E.g., combination of <u>ambrisentan</u> and <u>tadalafil</u>

* See “<u>Treatment of pulmonary hypertension</u>” and “<u>Acute decompensation of PAH</u>.”

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u>: <u>systemic immunomodulatory medications</u>, e.g., <u>mycophenolate mofetil</u> (See “<u>Management of ILD</u>.”)





> [!WARNING]
> Screen all patients for <u>signs of respiratory distress</u> as this can signify cardiopulmonary disease.




> [!TIP]
> Systemic <u>sclerosis</u> is a cause of <u>group 1 pulmonary hypertension</u>, so affected individuals are likely to benefit from <u>pulmonary vasodilators</u>. [[17]](/library/eycxVU0)




### Gastrointestinal disease [[6]](/library/wxchAe0)[[8]](/library/KxcUxe0)[[17]](/library/eycxVU0)




* <u>GERD</u>: <u>proton pump inhibitors</u> (<u>PPIs</u>)

* <u>GI motility disorder</u>: <u>prokinetic</u> therapy, e.g., <u>metoclopramide</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* <u>SIBO</u>: <u>antibiotic therapy</u>, e.g., <u>rifaximin</u> (<u>off-label</u>)
